findings.title: Case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? allows bypassing blocked emails
findings.body: `BlockedEmail` neither normalizes `email` (e.g., via `Email.downcase`) before saving nor downcases the input `email` in `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` before querying `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`. Because PostgreSQL `varchar` equality comparisons are case-sensitive, an entry blocking `bad@spammers.org` can be bypassed simply by signing up with `Bad@spammers.org`.

findings.title: Mutating match_count during validation double-counts on account creation
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the record inside `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs on every `valid?` call. In `UsersController#create` (lines 168 and 172), `user.valid?` is evaluated first and `user.save` is then called unconditionally (which runs validations a second time). As a result, every signup attempt in `UsersController#create` executes `BlockedEmail.should_block?` twice and increments `match_count` by 2 instead of 1.

findings.title: Unanchored domain regex in email_in_restriction_setting? allows whitelist bypass and false positives
findings.body: `EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting?` builds `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` without anchoring the match to the end of the address (`\z`). If `email_domains_whitelist` contains `example.com`, an address such as `user@example.com.attacker.com` will match and bypass the whitelist; conversely, if `email_domains_blacklist` contains `mail.com`, legitimate addresses such as `user@mail.company.org` will be falsely rejected.
